lede: Charge flows round a circuit whenever it is switched on, and the current tells you how fast. This topic puts a number on how much charge has flowed, in coulombs, and shows what happens to the voltage when cells are joined end to end, including one put in the wrong way round.
can: Calculate charge, current or time with Q = I × t
Convert minutes or hours to seconds before substituting
Work out the voltage of cells in series, allowing for a reversed cell

md: Switch on a torch and charge flows round its circuit. The current says how fast. Know how fast and for how long, and you know how much charge has passed. Join cells end to end and their voltages add, but only if they face the same way.

md:
**Charge** is measured in **coulombs (C)**. **Current** is the charge passing a point each second, measured in **amperes (A)**: 1 A means 1 coulomb every second.
So the charge that passes is the current multiplied by the time:
**charge = current × time**, or $Q = I \times t$

**Each second.** 0.4 coulombs pass the counter.
**For 180 seconds.** Q = 0.4 × 180 = 72 C.

prompt: A current of 2 A flows for 5 s. How much charge passes a point in the circuit, in coulombs?
explain: Every second 2 coulombs pass the point, and the current flows for 5 seconds, so multiply, as with the counter: Q = I × t = 2 × 5 = 10 C.

md:
A lamp does not use up charge. It takes **energy** from the charge passing through it, and the same coulombs flow on round the circuit and back to the cell.
**Counter 1.** In 3 minutes, 0.4 × 180 = 72 C flow into the lamp.
**Counter 2.** The same 72 C flow out of it.
That is why the current is the same all the way round a single loop.

prompt: A lamp in a circuit lights up. What happens to the charge that flows through the lamp?
options: it carries on round the circuit and back to the cell
it is used up by the lamp
it is stored inside the lamp
answer: it carries on round the circuit and back to the cell
explain: Look at the two counters: the charge into the lamp and the charge out of it are the same, 72 C. The lamp takes energy from the charge, not the charge itself, so the charge carries on round the circuit and back to the cell.

title: Why the time must be in seconds
md: Because the ampere is defined per second: one ampere is one coulomb every second. Put a time in minutes into $Q = I \times t$ and the answer comes out 60 times too small.

Convert on a line of its own, before anything is substituted:
**Minutes.** Multiply by 60: 20 min = 20 × 60 = 1200 s
**Hours.** Multiply by 3600: 2 h = 2 × 3600 = 7200 s

title: What examiners saw
md: **Summer 2025 Foundation:** in an electrical calculation, a significant minority did not convert 10 minutes into seconds and lost marks for it. The same slip was reported in Summer 2024.

prompt: A heater is switched on for 2.5 minutes. How many seconds is that?
explain: Each minute is 60 seconds, as on the scale above, so multiply by 60: 2.5 × 60 = 150 s. Half a minute is 30 seconds, so the decimal is no problem once you multiply.

md:
**Question.** A phone charges with a current of 1.5 A for 20 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows. [4]
**Step 1: the equation.** Q = I × t
**Step 2: time in seconds.** t = 20 × 60 = 1200 s
**Step 3: substitute.** Q = 1.5 × 1200 = 1800
**Step 4: the unit.** Q = 1800 C

md:
The same equation rearranges two ways:
**current = charge ÷ time**, $I = Q \div t$
**time = charge ÷ current**, $t = Q \div I$
Write the rearranged equation as your first line.

**The current, from the counter above.** 600 C in 4 minutes. Convert first: 4 × 60 = 240 s. Then I = 600 ÷ 240 = 2.5 A.
**A time.** 150 C delivered at 0.5 A: t = 150 ÷ 0.5 = 300 s.

prompt: A charge of 90 C passes through a heater in 45 s. What is the current, in amperes?
explain: The current is the charge passing each second, so divide the charge by the time, as with the counter above: I = Q ÷ t = 90 ÷ 45 = 2 A. The time was already in seconds.

caption: A cell turned round pushes against the others, so its voltage is subtracted.

md:
A cell turned the wrong way round pushes against the others, so its voltage is **subtracted**.
**Two cells, one reversed.** 1.5 − 1.5 = 0 V, and a lamp joined to them stays off.
**Three cells, middle reversed.** 1.5 − 1.5 + 1.5 = 1.5 V, the voltage of one cell.

prompt: Four 1.5 V cells are joined in series, and one of them is the wrong way round. What is the total voltage, in volts?
explain: As in the strings above, the cells facing the same way add and the reversed one subtracts: 1.5 + 1.5 − 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 V. The reversed cell cancels one of the others.

task: Join two batteries end to end with a light bulb to make a loop, and put a voltmeter across the two batteries. Read the voltmeter. Now select one battery and reverse it. Watch the voltmeter and the bulb. The simulation has no charge counter, so it cannot check Q = I × t; use it for the cells.

md: With both batteries the same way round, the voltmeter reads their voltages added. Reverse one and the reading falls to zero: the two push equally in opposite directions, so nothing drives a current and the bulb goes out.

prompt: Two 9 V batteries are joined in series and one is turned round. What does a voltmeter across both of them read, in volts?
explain: The two batteries push equally in opposite directions, as in the simulation, so one voltage takes away the other: 9 − 9 = 0 V, and the bulb goes out.

md: **Boxes for + and −.** Summer 2022, 2023 and 2025 Foundation drew a cell or battery with empty boxes to mark its polarity. Put + beside the long thin plate and − beside the short thick one.

**The current is on a label.** Summer 2024 printed a drill's information plate, with its current, voltage and frequency, and asked for the charge. Take only the value in amperes: 4 A for 30 s gives Q = 4 × 30 = 120 C.
**A huge current for a tiny time.** Summer 2021 Higher used a lightning flash. Type the time exactly as printed: 20 000 A for 0.001 s gives Q = 20 000 × 0.001 = 20 C.

prompt: A kettle's information plate reads: 230 V, 50 Hz, 2760 W, 12 A. The kettle is switched on for 90 s. Which line starts the charge calculation?
explain: Charge is current × time, and the current is the value in amperes, A, as with the drill above. The volts, hertz and watts on the plate are not needed for charge. So the first line is Q = 12 × 90, which gives 1080 C.

md:
Calculate charge with Q = I × t, and rearrange it for a current or a time.
Put a time in minutes or hours into seconds before you substitute.
Say what 1 A means: one coulomb past a point each second, all round the loop.
Add cells in series, subtracting any cell that faces the wrong way.
Take the current off an information plate; mark + at the long thin plate.

Charge usually comes as one part of a longer electricity question, worth [4]: the equation, the substitution, the answer and the unit C. The first mark is for writing Q = I × t before any number; if the time is in minutes, converting it is part of the working. Cells in series come with a diagram: check which way each cell faces before adding. Stuck? Write the equation and put the time into seconds.
